utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Good morning, everyone. Yes, good morning, Mr. Harvey.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. President, Your Honours. May I introduce Mireille Morsink, who is working for her masters in public administration at the university of Leiden who has been with my team for the last month and will be for a while to come. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Very well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Salipur.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Gaynor.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Mr. Salipur, in your statement at paragraph 8, you say that Crisis Staffs were formed in Serbian municipalities in accordance with a document dated the 26th of April, 1992. Now, it's right, isn't it, that the Crisis Staff were formed in municipalities by the SDS many months before April 1992?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SALIPUR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it depends. Throughout Bosnia-Herzegovina, Crisis Staff were being established, some earlier, others later, depending on how the situation developed in the field. In some places it simply wasn't necessary to have one, depended on the structure of the population, and also if perhaps certain incidents had already occurred. So dates are different in different municipalities.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Now, in your statement at paragraph 5 you say that you do not know the document entitled "Instructions for the activity of the Serbian people in extraordinary circumstances (variant A and B)." Now, it's right, isn't it, that that --

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SALIPUR [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I've never heard of this variant A and B. Actually, I hadn't heard of it until I heard about it through the media when this Tribunal started dealing with these matters. Before that I had never heard of this variant, although I'm some kind of participant in all of these events as far as the Serbian Democratic Party is concerned from when it was founded up until the war. Although I was close to sources of information in Sarajevo, I never heard of this variant. I certainly have not heard of it, and I do not know of its existence if it did exist in the first place.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Do you accept that you personally participated in the implementation of instructions received from the SDS Main Board in December 1991?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SALIPUR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did participate, but at the same time, I was the legitimate representative of the people and citizens, because at the first multi-party elections, I was elected a member of the Municipal Assembly. That was our task, to take care of security as part of overall life and Crisis Staffs were the result of all of that, as was everything else.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Can I call up, please, P5.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: The document that's on the screen in front of you, Mr. Salipur, states in the top left-hand corner "Serbian Democratic Party, Bosnia-Herzegovina Main Board." It is dated at the bottom the 19th of December, 1991. If we turn to the second page, you can see the foot of the document a reference to variant A, and underneath variant A you see two words. Could you read out those two words, please.

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SALIPUR [Resumed]
utterances.text: "And co-operation with all local committees in the area of the municipality." Is that what you meant, where it says "First Level"?

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Yes, the two words "First Level" I want you to keep those in mind. Now, if we turn to the next page of this document we see a list of tasks numbered 1 to 5, and then if we turn to the next page, tasks go on from 6 to 11, and they stop at 11. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SALIPUR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: May I call up, please, P2575.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: You can see this document is a record of a Crisis Staff meeting held on the premises of the Novo Sarajevo Serbian Democratic Party. The meeting heard and discussed the materials received from the SDS BH Main Board. Underneath that you see two words. Do you see those two words? Under "SDS BiH."

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SALIPUR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I see that. May I explain?

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Can you read out those two words, please.

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SALIPUR [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Material received from the Main Board of the Serb Democratic Party of Bosnia-Herzegovina."

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: And the next two words.

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SALIPUR [Resumed]
utterances.text: "First Level."

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: That's the exactly the same expression as you saw in the previous document, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SALIPUR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I understand, but in this document there is absolutely no mention of any variant A or variant B. "First level" is one word. As for variant A and B, I don't know what those words mean. I have to correct you. This is a meeting of the Crisis Staff of the Municipal Board, municipal. So that is the lowest-ranking cell in the party, if you can put it that way. We received this from the Main Board of the SDS. We received the complete material, and that is what you previously put to me. You put this to me. I really don't see. After all, if I can remember correctly --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpret did not understand the rest of the sentence.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In line 12 it says that "we did receive," where the witness said, "we did not receive."

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, did you receive material from the Main Board of the SDS?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SALIPUR [Resumed]
utterances.text: We received instructions on activity which is a succinct part of the material that you put here, and as for that page and mentioning variant A and B, I mean the first time I heard of this variant A and B was -- well, I know as far as looking at the situation, you know, first level and things like that, and then this second one was envisaged, but then that was materialised through the war, and then there was no need for the first one anyway.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Now, in this document you will see there are items numbered 1, 2, 3, there is no item 4 or 5, and then there are items 6, 7, 8, 9, and 11. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SALIPUR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Now, your name in full appears under item 11, and the name Salipur appears under item 6. So you were responsible for implementing items 6 and 11, weren't you?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SALIPUR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Now, you worked with Radomir Neskovic, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SALIPUR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Neskovic is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. Sorry to interrupt you, Mr. Gaynor, but we need to clarify this a bit more precisely. Mr. Salipur, this is your answer to the question of Mr. Gaynor asking about this document which is in front of you now. I read out the answer as translated: "This is a meeting of the Crisis Staff of the Municipal Board, municipal. So that's the lowest-ranking cell in the party, if you can put that way. We received this from the Main Board of the SDS. We received the complete material, and that is what you previously put to me." Then -- and that was your answer. Mr. Karadzic stated that the sentence "we received the complete material" should be translated as "we didn't receive the complete material." But before that when you are saying about the meeting of the lowest-ranking cell, you did say that you received this from the Main Board of the SDS. So what I understand from your further answer to Mr. Gaynor, you received some -- some material in a succinct form from the Main Board, but you didn't receive the complete set of document. Is that what you're going -- what you said?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, precisely. We received extracts from that document. If you look at all of this, this is some kind of instruction as to how to act in some kind of situation that crops up.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. You received the extracts from that document. Did you see those extracts yourself?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, I did not. The conduct and work in the party was such that all material that arrived, when meetings would be held, the person chairing the meeting would read out a document, and then there would be a debate, discussion, and certain conclusions would be reached. Other members absolutely do not look at the document, only the official that works for the Municipal Board.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Then how did you know that only the extracts had been received at the time instead of the whole set of documents?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Because the person who was chairing the meeting tells us and says, We received instructions on further activity in a deteriorated critical situation, and does not communicate the entire document. He communicates to us what he received.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Back to you, Mr. Gaynor.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Witness, you can see this is dated the 23rd of December, 1991, which is four days after the variant A and B document.

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SALIPUR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Now, Radomir Neskovic gave evidence before this Trial Chamber, the reference is T14353. He told this Trial Chamber: "This document is not a forgery. It is a document of the Crisis Staff of Novo Sarajevo. Based on the contents, it is variant A. So variant A is being applied here." Do you accept that this document is, in fact, implementing variant A of the variant A and B instructions even if you personally had not seen a copy of the variant A and B instructions?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SALIPUR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Number one, Mr. Radomir Neskovic at the time of all of this did not participate personally as I did, and he certainly could not have determined which came -- what came as a result of what, and his name would be here among the other names. It would be on the other documents, I mean of members of the Municipal Board and thing like that, and I don't know how come he judged it that way. I'm saying again that this is the first level of conduct on the basis of instructions. We received instructions on how we should behave in the situation that prevailed at that time. The situation was already rather chaotic. Different things were happening, incidents. There were all sorts of songs that were being sung that the Croatian borders on the Drina. There were also the green flags, and we had to act in some way so that there would not be greater unrest. We had to see how we should act. There is nothing bad about these duties of ours. There are no intentions or preparations for war.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Now, you accept that the name Radomir Neskovic does appear on this document under item 8?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SALIPUR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, now I do notice his name, but now whether this has to do with the one that I have in mind, I'm not sure. I know that later after the war broke out he took over the Crisis Staff of the municipality, and he was appointed by the Government of Republika Srpska. That I do know. As for this pre-war period, I don't know that he participated.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Can I call up, please, 65 ter 01477.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: As you can see, this is a record of a Crisis Staff meeting held on the 25th of December, 1991, two days after the previous Crisis Staff meeting. This document lists a series of tasks which are assigned. Under item 3 we can see that a task has been assigned to you. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SALIPUR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Number 3? I see that. I don't know what you're interested in. What you'd want me to explain about this task that I was entrusted with, what it had to do with or what I was supposed to do in relation to this task.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: You accepted the Crisis Staff was issuing instructions to various members on the 25th of December, 1991?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SALIPUR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Number 1, the Crisis Staff consists of ten members of the secretariat of the Municipal Board, and the others are from the Serbian Democratic Party, and they worked as appointed officials in the municipality; that is to say the Crisis Staff had a mixed composition, and it cannot be considered to be an independent body. It could not have done anything independently without the Municipal Board knowing about this and the officials who worked in the municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: And the Crisis Staff, when you say it was not an independent body, it was receiving instructions from above, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SALIPUR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes. That's why I said that the composition was mixed, that it wasn't some kind of separate institution or separate organisation.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Now, you said at the beginning of your evidence the Crisis Staffs had been formed pursuant to a document from April 1992. Do you accept on the basis of this document and the previous document we saw that the Crisis Staff was in fact formed at least as early as December 1991?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: I think it's misleading.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, you take up the issue in your re-examination. The witness has already answered. Shall we move on?

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: I'd just like to clarify. Witness, when you said, "Yes," you were saying yes to my question; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SALIPUR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the question was whether the Crisis Staff had been established already towards the end -- the end -- the end of 1991, and we have to Crisis Staff that appears in some documents in the beginning of the war. Those two -- I mean the composition of persons in these two Crisis Staffs are quite different and the tasks are quite different, because the war had broken out and many members moved away. They went in different directions. So if we can refer to this as continuity of work, it did exist up to a point but with different people in a different situation, because the war had already started, whereas this was the pre-war situation. I can tell you that even if we had not received any instructions from the Main Staff, we would have done all of these same things at the Municipal Board. We would have carried out all these tasks, because they were not aimed against anyone, not aimed against other peoples, just to ensure greater safety and security, more order, sufficient food supplies if a war breaks out for persons who had not had sufficient care, and also in individual homes and families so that if a war were to break out there wouldn't be famine, a breakdown law and order. Then also there should be lists of the disabled and the sickly so that they could be assisted. No one knew what kind of war would start and when.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Mr. President, I would like to tender 65 ter 01477.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. We will receive it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BAIRD
utterances.text: But, Mr. Gaynor, Dr. Karadzic, I think that we should have this matter clarified before we go further. Now, the question you asked, Mr. Gaynor, some time ago was this: "Do you accept that on the basis of this document and previous documents that the Crisis Staff was, in fact, formed as early as December 1991?" Now, at that point, Mr. Karadzic, you had objected to the question on the ground that it was misleading. Am I right?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, your Excellency.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BAIRD
utterances.text: Now, was this matter addressed at all, Mr. Gaynor? Do you recollect that?

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Yes, I asked the witness to clarify if he had answered yes to my question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BAIRD
utterances.text: And he gave this answer, this long answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BAIRD
utterances.text: Is this an answer to the question?

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Well, I can show him one final document and then I can return to the point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BAIRD
utterances.text: Thank you very much, indeed. Yes, I'd appreciate this.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Thank you. Could we call up, please, P2583.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Before doing that, shall we give the number for this exhibit?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Document 1477 receives number P6055, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: Excellencies, may I in English explain why it is misleading so that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Shall we continue?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BAIRD
utterances.text: Let us proceed, Mr. Gaynor, for the time being, shall we?

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Now, on the document -- on the screen in front of you, Mr. Witness, you see a record of the minutes of the Crisis Staff staff meeting held in Lukavica community on the 29th of January, 1992, among those attending is Radomir Neskovic. Under item 4 it states: "Zdravko Salipur has fully completed the task relating to the municipal vehicles." Do you see that, Mr. Witness?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SALIPUR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do. I do, and I can briefly explain something about this task that says that I in a very brief period of time was the only one to carry out my task. My task at the time had to do with the following: There was a shortage of fuel for vehicles at the time, and the municipality and the town Assembly issued special coupons so you couldn't buy fuel with money. Since I worked in the municipality in order to provide fuel, obtain fuel and coupons for vehicles, fuel that came from Novo Sarajevo, and I knew how we could work as an institution, as a political party, in accordance with the law, and we could also obtain some of those coupons in accordance with the law and we could use them for fuel. So this was my task. I carried it out expeditiously. There were no ill intentions when this was done. Mr. Radomir Neskovic had some duties in the municipality. He was the director for the housing fund that the municipality has, and in relation to that, he was probably involved in this issue in case special accommodation was required.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Now, under item 1 it says that stations are to be taken over by Milenko Jovanovic and Zdravko Salipur on behalf of the Crisis Staff. Can you tell us what that is a reference to?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SALIPUR [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the time, there were no mobile phones. As the Municipal Board, we obtained a number of small radio -- hand-held radio devices, ones that radio ham operators use so that individual members could at any point in time, if they weren't somewhere where there was a land-line, maintain contact. They were distributed to some members of the Municipal Boards, and then we obtained information according to which they just call each other, tell jokes to each other, speak to each other by using these devices, so we decided to take them back from them, and later we were to see to whom we might distribute these devices.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Now, I have shown you this morning a record of a Crisis Staff meeting held on the premises of the Novo Sarajevo SDS to discuss materials received from the SDS Main Board. That meeting was on the 23rd of December, 1991. I showed you another document of a Crisis Staff meeting held on the 25th of December, 1991. I showed you a third document which are the minutes of the Crisis Staff meeting held on the 29th of January, 1991. On the basis of those documents, you must accept that the SDS had formed a Crisis Staff in your municipality at least as early as December 1991.

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SALIPUR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, if you noticed, in one of the documents there are some members from the staff who assigned tasks to co-ordinate activities between the Crisis Staff of the SDS and the HDZ of Bosnia-Herzegovina. So in other political parties there were already Crisis Staffs in existence. They had been established before we established ours. We named the coordinators in documents so that they could be interlocutors. This was done so that we could calm down the situation as much as possible to defuse tension, if you will.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: One final question. You must accept, yes or no, that the SDS did establish the Crisis Staff in Novo Sarajevo municipality at least as early as December 1991? Yes or no?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SALIPUR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes, but in the context that I've mentioned in my answers, all of my answers, have a look at one of the earlier documents where it says that we have a coordinator for contact with other Crisis Staffs.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: In your statement at paragraph 5, you say that Radovan Karadzic, President of the SDS, attended the pre-war sessions of your SDS Municipal Board meetings. About how many did he attend?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SALIPUR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Since the Novo Sarajevo municipality is essential one in the town of Sarajevo and the town consisted of eight municipalities, apart from the Municipal Board there was a working group called the town board, because the authorities in Sarajevo had a town Assembly and Municipal Assembly, so no deputies in the Municipal Assemblies and the town Assemblies. The headquarters of the town board of the Serbian Democratic Party was in Novo Sarajevo and that was also the case for the Municipal Board. President Karadzic attended meetings of the town board more frequently, because you had deputies, representatives from all the town, from all the eight municipalities, one could say, and sometimes he would also attend our meetings of the Municipal Board. Unfortunately, we often had internal tensions, and he had to come to calm us down so we could solve our problems, and so on and so forth. So I don't know how many times that was, in fact, but he had a lot of duties to perform, but at least ten times from the elections, from the time the elects were held, up until the time when the war broke out.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The witness said "reconcile," not "calm down." And the witness said that there was co-operation with the Crisis Staffs of the HDZ and the SDA, and SDA isn't there. He said "to reconcile us."

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Now, at paragraph 6, you note that when the war broke out, Dr. Karadzic left Sarajevo for Pale. Do you accept that Dr. Karadzic remained in close contact with members of the Municipal Board, the SDS Municipal Board, of Novo Sarajevo while he was in Pale and after he had moved to Pale?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SALIPUR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it seems -- he didn't go there on his own. All our political leadership, all our party leadership from Sarajevo went there. Pale isn't very far from Novo Sarajevo municipality which had its own territory. Life had to go on. It was necessary to co-operate, to establish the authorities of government. This was all done. And to do that, naturally he had to have contact with our municipality and people who acted as leaders in the municipality. During the first month when the war broke out, as soon as the government had been formed in the territory of Republika Srpska, the party's work was frozen for one year. That was the decision, because one wanted to have unity prevail amongst the people, and one wanted to prepare a better defence within the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Do you know Rajko Bajic, Dragan Vucetic and Slavko Aleksic?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SALIPUR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Were they all members of the SDS Municipal Board of Novo Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SALIPUR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Aleksic, yes. And Rajko Bajic was a prominent member of the party, but I don't think he was a member of the Municipal Board. I'm not certain about that. And Dragan Vucetic, yes, he was a member of the Municipal Board and he worked in Novo Sarajevo municipality. He was an urban inspector. That was the position he held, and he had a permanent job there.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: And do you accept that you remained in contact with other members of the Municipal Board of Sarajevo and with the leadership in Pale?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SALIPUR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Do you have me in mind or the Municipal Board as a whole?

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: The Municipal Board as a whole.

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SALIPUR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, I lived at the other end of town in relation to the territory of the Serbian municipality of Novo Sarajevo, or it was that municipality when the war broke out, and to be more specific in the settlement of Pofalica. It was war. I had contact in relation to the party, and so on and so forth, up until the beginning of the war, and from then onwards I wasn't free to move around. My neighbourhood was mainly inhabited by Serbs. We organised ourselves, organised guards as well so as to avoid unpleasant scenes. Unfortunately, this didn't last for long. On the 16th of May, 1992, the Muslim forces attacked our settlement, our neighbourhood, or, rather, one of the enclaves as one might call it, and on that occasion I was seriously wounded. I went away for treatment. I returned from treatment in Belgrade late in the autumn of 1992. So as for the other events from the 4th of April up until October, did I not participate in those events. All I know is what I know through rumours, but I wasn't a direct participant in the events, and I know nothing about them.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Can I call up please 65 ter 01463.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: This is a document dated the 8th of August, 1992. I accept that you were in Belgrade at that time. Now, in this document which is signed by Dr. Radovan Karadzic, you can read it for yourself, sir, but I think we can see that Dr. Karadzic is summoning Rajko Bajic, Dragan Vucetic and Slavko Aleksic to report to him in person.

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SALIPUR [Resumed]
utterances.text: The date is the 8th of August, 912. It doesn't say 1992. It says 912 here, but the translation in English says "Sarajevo, the 8th of August, 1992."

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Yes, very well observed, Mr. Salipur. I think we can accept that's a typographical error and it should read 8th of the 8th, 1992. Now, do you -- do you agree that President Karadzic --

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SALIPUR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't understand. It says Sarajevo, the 8th of August, 1992. President Karadzic in August 1992 wasn't in Sarajevo. He was in Pale. It should say Pale and then you should have the date. I don't know. I never heard that they had authority of any kind. See how the municipality was working. As far as I know, Milenko Jovanovic in that part of Sarajevo was seriously wounded in both legs in Vraca, and he spent more time being treated than I did, almost a year. So this is completely illogical to me.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Has the possibility of the year being 1991 been considered? There should be a 2 under the number, because we put a dot after numbers.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That would sooner be like that, because I know that they received something from you in 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: In any event, setting the date of this document to one side for a moment, you accept that Dr. Karadzic was in personal contact with Slavko Aleksic and the two other men named in this document?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SALIPUR [Resumed]
utterances.text: In your earlier question as to whether I knew Bajic Rajko, Slavko Aleksic, I said yes, Aleksic was a member of the Municipal Board. Vucetic, Dragan was a member of the Municipal Board and Bajic, Rajko was a prominent member of the party. I am not sure. I don't think he was in the Municipal Board. As I had mentioned earlier on I know that we had some tension, some disagreements, and so on, about certain matters, and in 1991 on one occasion President Karadzic authorised them to carry out an inventory of the equipment because there was a dispute, an internal dispute. It was said that someone had spent money in an inappropriate manner, something like that, and Rajko Bajic is an economist, I think. Mr. Jovanovic, he worked in the Ministry of the Interior, didn't he? They wanted to deal with the matter. I think the document might have to do with this and I believe that it was in 1991. It says an inventory of all the equipment or materiel.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: You told us that Aleksic was a member of the Municipal Board. Aleksic was also a Vojvoda who led volunteer units of the Serbian Chetnik detachment, wasn't he?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SALIPUR [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I returned from my treatment I lived in Grbavica, a hundred metres from the demarcation line which was being secured by a company under the command of Slavko Aleksic. He was a regular member of the Army of Republika Srpska in terms of establishment. He had a bit of a beard and was called a Vojvoda. Well, that's a totally different matter. But he wasn't a volunteer of any kind. You will find his name in the documents of the Municipal Board when the party was established, from the time the party was established up until the time the war broke out and his pre-war address was at the location where the demarcation line was, where he was the company commander in Gornji Kovacici. So he wasn't a volunteer of any kind. He was a local inhabitant. He was born from Bileca. But he left Bileca and came to Sarajevo at least ten years prior to the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Thank you. I'm going to have to move on because I'm under some time pressure.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Could I tender the document on the screen, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Any objection, Mr. Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, we will receive it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 1463 receives P6056, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Could I call up, please, P5035.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Document which is come up is dated the 13th of May, 1993. It's an order of the Serbian Chetnik Movement. And we can see under item 1 of this document that Slavko Aleksic is named, and there is a reference to his activity as commander of the Novo Sarajevo Chetnik Detachment. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SALIPUR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Could I also call up, please, 65 ter number 23871.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: The next document is a receipt dated the 5th of January, 1994 - you will see it in a moment - signed by Vojvoda Slavko Aleksic, confirming receipt of documents from RS MUP Ilidza SJB. Do you see that, Mr. Witness?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SALIPUR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Do you accept, therefore, that Aleksic was a commander of the Novo Sarajevo Chetnik Detachment and received weapons from the Bosnian Serb police force?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SALIPUR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me repeat what I said. I'm claiming with full responsibility that in spite of everything that you have known, in spite of all these documents that you have shown, the unit under the command of Slavko Aleksic in the war was a company that was part -- I'm not sure whether it was the 1st or 2nd Battalion. For a time it was the Sarajevo and later the Romanija Motorised Brigade. Also in this document where it says "Received," Pajic, Veljko. He was also a member of the Army of Republika Srpska and a company commander at a demarcation line which continued from the zone which was under the control of Slavko Aleksic. And let me go back to what I said. From the time the party was established up until the war broke out, he was a member of the Municipal Board of the SDS. Well, Chetnik detachment and so on and so forth, that has nothing to do with it. You can see under whose command he operated.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: I'd like to tender that document, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Could you ask the witness to read out the stamp? Can we zoom in the stamp we can see at the bottom of the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Are you able to read any of those stamps, Mr. Witness?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The stamps which we see at the bottom of the document. Can you -- yes. English translation says -- it reads "Vojvoda Slavko Aleksic." Do you agree?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I agree with the translation. I can see these letters, but it's not clear to me that a stamp could only have the name of a -- of a man. What is he? What's his position? Which organ does he belong to? It's the first time in my 65 years that I've seen a stamp with just a first and last name and nothing else. Have a look above. "Goods received by. Goods issued by." Slavko Aleksic's name doesn't appear there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. We'll receive this.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 23871 receives number P6057, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Now, in your evidence yesterday -- I'm moving to a separate topic, Mr. Witness. This concerns the Zehra Muidovic maternity hospital. In your evidence yesterday you said at page 31623: "All the media, all the propaganda that I heard stated that at the beginning of the war we shelled the maternity war and destroyed it." And you went on to confirm that you were talking about the maternity ward at Zehra Muidovic hospital. Then you were asked by Dr. Karadzic, "Did we destroy that maternity ward?" And you answered, "No, it wasn't destroyed." Now, do you accept that the Zehra Muidovic maternity hospital was not destroyed at the time that your son became a father but that it was later shelled and destroyed?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SALIPUR [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, it wasn't my son who became a father. I became a father. I had a son. That is the first correction. My son was born on the 20th of April in that maternity ward. My wife used to work in the maternity ward for 14 years before the war. Until that day, not a single pane of glass was shattered on the building, let alone that the building was shelled. People worked there safely. I took my wife there to deliver and picked her up three days later. Due to security reasons, because the maternity ward was close to the separation line during the war, it was transferred to another hospital, and in the maternity ward UNPROFOR and other international forces were billeted. Was it the SFOR? I don't know. They kept changing their name. So it wasn't shelled, and especially not while they were there and not before either. Where would they have been billeted if it had been destroyed? That's the real situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: I want to focus on the period after you had been transferred to Belgrade for medical treatment, and I want to put it to you that while you were away from Sarajevo, the shell -- the maternity hospital was shelled and in fact was destroyed.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Could we call up, please, 65 ter 24365.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: This is a story of the Associated Press. Now, Mr. Witness, it's only available in the English language so I'll tell you what it is. The title is "In Sarajevo, the hospital is a dangerous place." It's dated the 16th of August, 1992, and in the fourth paragraph it says and I quote: "Already the Zehra Muidovic maternity hospital located near the front line of fighting between Serbian and Bosnian forces has been destroyed. During the fighting, three babies - two in incubators - died." Now, do you accept that by 16th of August, 1992, the Zehra Muidovic maternity hospital had been destroyed?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The witness is asked to speculate because the witness stated he wasn't there at the time.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I wasn't there at the time, but I think this is mere propaganda.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: So you're suggesting that the Associated Press is acting as a propaganda organ for the Bosnian government. Is that your position? Mr. Witness, you can answer the question.

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SALIPUR [Resumed]
utterances.text: You see, I didn't quite understand, because you were speaking in a low key, but there were two babies, some in incubators and other people who were hurt. How come they were hurt whereas none of the staff taking care of the babies were wounded? I guess they didn't flee leaving the babies behind. This is a propaganda report, nothing more. I'm simply using my logic. And I'm not saying this because I was present.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: I'd now like to move to a video. There are four extracts, and they'll run for a total of about two minutes and 20 seconds. Before we play that I'd like to tender the Associated Press article.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Gaynor, the Chamber is of the view that given the fact that the relevant part of the document has been read out and reflected in full in the transcript, it's not necessary to receive it.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you, Mr. President. The video is taken from radio television Bosnia and Herzegovina. These are four extracts, so for the sake of the record, I'll read them out as we play them. The first is from 3 minutes and 41 seconds to 4 minutes and 25 seconds.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: We are reading out the transcript received from the Prosecution: "Srecko Simic: We survived a very difficult night - the night for which I still cannot believe could happen in a civilised world. The horrors that our pregnant women, our child-bearing women, our mothers, our newly-born babies, our ... the female and male patients of our clinic."

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: The second extract is from 5 minutes and 6 seconds to 5 minutes and 26 seconds.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: "[Voiceover] The Sarajevo maternity ward, Zehra Muidovic today."

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: The third extract is 6 minutes and 28 seconds to 7 minutes and 6 seconds.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: "[Voiceover] Unknown man 2: There are some over here where the breast-feeding women are. These are the babies from the pediatrics."

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we get a time reference?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: "[Voiceover] Unknown man 1: Take footage of this over here."

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: The time reference is -- we believe this is from the 27th of May, 1992, for shelling on the night of the 26th of May, 1992. Third extract is from -- sorry, excuse me. The fourth extract is from 7 minutes and 50 seconds to 8 minutes and 28 seconds.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: "[Voiceover] Unknown man 2: It's a lucky thing that it did not start burning. "Unknown man 3: It did start burning, but it was extinguished. "Unknown man 3: Here, this part over here. Take a footage of this chaos. You see this here which was burnt? You can take footage from here."

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Witness, I put it to you that during the period you were receiving hospital treatment in Belgrade the Zehra Muidovic maternity hospital was in fact shelled, and you are not in a position to exclude the possibility that the VRS shelled the Zehra Muidovic maternity hospital.

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SALIPUR [Resumed]
utterances.text: My statement I depicted the true events. As for the propaganda that the maternity ward was shelled at the very beginning of the war and that my son was born on the 20th of April -- well, for the first period of the war, the maternity ward operated normally. I was wounded on the 16th of May, 1992, and transferred to Belgrade for treatment where I spent five months up. Until the 16th of May, I claim that there was no shelling. I was following the events in Sarajevo. I'm not certain about the period later. It is possible that it was destroyed when they moved out because of the immediate danger. I know this person who gave the statement and the footage, Professor Simic. Mr. Prosecutor, why don't you find out where Mr. Simic is now and when he left Sarajevo? Did he provide this statement under coercion? I have other information, because I know that man well. I have known him for ten years. It wasn't easy for him to be in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Now, from your evidence two things arise. First of all, you cannot exclude the possibility that the VRS shelled this hospital after the 16th of May, 1992, can you?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SALIPUR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: The second thing is --

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SALIPUR [Resumed]
utterances.text: But I have my doubts, which I have expressed.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: And the second thing is on the basis of the footage you've seen, you cannot exclude the possibility that the VRS shelled the Zehra Muidovic maternity hospital while there were patients in that hospital, including newborn babies?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SALIPUR [Resumed]
utterances.text: In any case, I exclude that possibility. In my view, the only possibility is that it was shelled perhaps the buildings of the maternity ward were shelled. When they left they went to the Kosevo Hospital. In my statement I said it was close to the separation line where it was dangerous in any case. It is possible that after that the building was used, and I had said in a previous statement that it was at an elevation. It was a vantage point. And perhaps when it was abandoned it was used by the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and perhaps that is why there were shells flying overhead occasionally hitting the building itself. That would be my final say on this topic.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: I have no further questions. I'd like to tender the four extracts, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. On what basis?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] First of all, your Excellencies, this witness was not there at the time and cannot confirm anything. Second of all, we do not have a clear time reference. We see that this was edited material created on different days. This is definitely propaganda material put together by the Sarajevo Television. Finally, we heard Dr. Pejic testify who said that the same person, Dr. Simic, handed over the hospital quite early on to the authorities and that they went to Kosevo.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: By the way, can I have the 65 ter number again, Mr. Gaynor?

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: For this video.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: The 65 ter number is 40171A. I should say that the video is available as V000-0351 and we could play far more extracts from this video if necessary. We can certainly make it available to the Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: You agree this is an edited version of Sarajevo -- from Sarajevo Television?

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: We agree it was broadcast on Radio Television Bosnia-Herzegovina, I believe. Now the footage would have been edited prior to being broadcast, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The Chamber will give its ruling after the break.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, do you have any re-examination?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, your Excellencies, a few questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Salipur, at the time when the Serb municipality of Novo Sarajevo was constituted where were you? When was it constituted, in April, on the 10th or the 12th, something like that?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SALIPUR [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the Assembly session when people were elected, that was at the beginning of the war. Is that the one you have in mind?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SALIPUR [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that moment in time, whoever was there in terms of deputies and committee members -- well, people were trying to set up civilian authorities as quickly as possible, so that session was held in the Lukavica municipal -- local commune. Dr. Prijic was appointed Assembly speaker, and Mr. Radan was President of the Executive Board. I wasn't present, but later on in my political work I came across that -- those documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you know, then, whether the municipality established a Crisis Staff as a state organ as opposed to it being a party organ?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SALIPUR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't say anything precisely. The Crisis Staff -- well, Neskovic was in charge of it. It's not clear to me. It didn't have the role of the Crisis Staff as we discussed it. It was completely -- a completely new thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Okay. We won't pursue that since you were not there. It was suggested to you that the Crisis Staff received instructions from above. Did the party Crisis Staff receive instructions from the Main Board or from its Municipal Board?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SALIPUR [Resumed]
utterances.text: From its Municipal Board.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Is it correct that -- well, when did the SDA and HDZ establish their Crisis Staff compared to the SDS?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SALIPUR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't say precisely, but definitely before the SDS Crisis Staff was established. That is why we tasked our people on the Crisis Staff, two people in particular, to co-ordinate work and communicate with the Crisis Staffs of the other two parties. It is in the minutes of the Crisis Staff meeting. People are known, those who were tasked with that. So they must have established their staffs before.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. During that period before the outbreak of the war, were you involved in this or were you doing anything covertly that would be hidden from the other parties and the public?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SALIPUR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think everything we did was undertaking obligations and it was no secret. It wasn't possible to do anything in secret. All of the organs were still mixed in terms of composition. If the head of a department was of one ethnicity and his deputy of another, well, how could it be secret then? That's as far as the municipal authorities go. As for party organs, everyone was cautious trying to gather as much information on the other side as possible. It was impossible to keep anything hidden or to act covertly.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. When the war broke out, well you were not there from the start, but when you arrived in the fall of 1992, what was the situation like in terms of telephone communication in Sarajevo between Pale and Novo Sarajevo and in general? How did the telephone network operate?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SALIPUR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the grid was not in the best of condition in terms of the town of Sarajevo which was controlled by Muslim forces. There were no telephone lines that could be used to communicate with Pale, only a few, but it was very difficult, because the telephone network was established in a different way before the war. It went through the main city switchboard and then to Pale, and later on there were only a few lines left going to Pale and they were constantly overcrowded.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Where was the main town switchboard in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SALIPUR [Resumed]
utterances.text: In Novo Sarajevo at Dolac Malta across the street from the municipal building of Novo Sarajevo before the war and close to the Catholic church, if you remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Who controlled that area when the war broke out?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SALIPUR [Resumed]
utterances.text: From day one to the last one, it was controlled by the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did they leave your telephone lines at your disposal?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SALIPUR [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You were shown my decision to carry out an inventory or create an inventory list of party property, and it was suggested that I was in indirect contact with Slavko Aleksic. In principle, was it necessary to be in contact with each and every person if a decision like that was to be issued to the Municipal Board?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SALIPUR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. President, before that decision you attended a meeting of ours. I believe I spoke at that meeting, asking you to reconcile our differences within the Municipal Board. There were mutual accusations at the time. After the meeting, you appointed three of them as members of the Municipal Board to make an inventory list so that all doubts would be removed that the people had. Money was involved, including membership fees of party members, voluntary contributions. It was about money for the most part and that's where people begin to argue the easiest.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Salipur. I ask this reluctantly, but I wanted to ask you about your opinion or your knowledge of me as a person and a party and State leader.

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SALIPUR [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is difficult for me to explain. It would take a long time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. While it may be relevant, how does it arise from the cross-examination, Mr. Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Excellency, it was suggested that I was in personal communication, that I issued instructions, that I meddled with the work of the Municipal Board and that nothing could go ahead without my knowledge. It was all suggested by my learned friend Mr. Gaynor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: But your question was formulated in a more general way.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'll narrow it down.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. Proceed, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Salipur, according to your knowledge, what was the nature of my activities vis-a-vis your municipality, the party, and the period before and during the war?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SALIPUR [Resumed]
utterances.text: In my statement, in the paragraph I mentioned this: When you came to visit and when we could see what was happening in the area of the former Yugoslavia, you were very optimistic that there would be no war in Bosnia-Herzegovina, especially not in Sarajevo. You encouraged us and you enjoyed a lot of respect, and whenever you came to attend a meeting or were there informally, we were always very happy to have you. You never seemed abrupt, wilful, or too critical or too stern. If you did criticise it was always with the aim of improving the situation. You were always telling us that things could be done better. You were a proponent of people not having several positions. You were against double hatting. You kept saying that people should not be in the board and in party, and I liked that in particular. I would have a lot to say about that. I could go on for days.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Salipur. I have no further questions of you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Salipur, that concludes your evidence. On behalf of the Chamber, I thank you for coming to The Hague to give it. Now you are free to go, but we'll rise all together. We'll have a break for half an hour.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Excellencies, may I introduce a new member of our team.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. We have with us today Nadja Hayman Jelenkovic of Serbian Chinese dissent from Hong Kong.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Would the witness take the solemn declaration, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Stanic. Please be seated and make yourself comfortable. Before you proceed, Mr. Karadzic, the Chamber will now issue its oral ruling on the admission of 65 ter 4017A. Having considered the parties' submissions, the Chamber is of the view that the provenance and the date of the video had not been sufficiently established for the purpose of admission. The Chamber further notes that the witness was not able to further comment on this point or on any other matter depicted in the video. The Chamber will therefore not admit 65 ter 4017A into evidence. Yes, Mr. Karadzic, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good day, Mr. Stanic.

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR STANIC
utterances.text: Good day, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I would kindly ask you to speak slowly as I should. Also let us pause between questions and answers so that the interpreters manage to interpret everything we say and that it's all reflected in the record.

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR STANIC
utterances.text: Fine. No problem.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did you give the Defence team a statement?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR STANIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Just pause a bit, please.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 1D6725, could we have that in e-court, please. 1D6725.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Shall we switch it to e-court. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Is this the statement that you gave to the Defence team?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR STANIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you read this statement and did you sign it?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR STANIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. I read it and I signed it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Does this statement accurately reflect everything you said?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR STANIC
utterances.text: Everything is recorded the way I remember it and the way I put it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: If I were to put the same questions to you today in court, would your answers be the same?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR STANIC
utterances.text: I hope so. If they are written in this statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Excellencies, I would like to tender this statement according to 92 ter, and there are no associated exhibits except for an additional one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, we'll admit it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 1D6725 receives number D2678, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Now I would like to read out a brief summary of Mr. Stanic's statement. I'll read it out in English. [In English] Svetozar Stanisic was born on 26 of December, 1945, in the village of Dubljevici, Gacko municipality. He completed his primary school in Vogosca and then attend the secondary school in Sarajevo where he also obtained a university degree at the faculty of forestry. He worked in Sipad Inzenjering in Sarajevo until 6 of April, 1992. Mr. Svetozar Stanic was a deputy in the Vogosca Municipal Assembly and a member of the Vogosca Crisis Staff. After the events of March 1992, the assassination of a Serbian wedding guest, inter-ethnic tensions escalated drastically. The Serbian people felt threatened because the MUP Ministry of Interior in Sarajevo harboured the organisers and perpetrators of this act. Members of the SDS found the legal basis for the formation of the Serbian municipality of Vogosca in the BH Constitution and the SDS created this, which was constituted in March 1992. In doing this, the SDS adhered to the legal basis and the law of ONO. That means All People's Defence. Svetozar Stanic considers that the directive or plan A and B is a response to the decision of the government of the Republic of BH in the regionalisation of BH. It was intended as a reminder to municipal authorities of the provisions of the Law on National Defence, All People's Defence, and relevant sections of the constitution. Until mid-April 1992, there were no problems with inter-ethnic relations in Vogosca. However, in mid-April of 1992, the Muslim forces, completely unprovoked, surrendered an unarmed civilian settlement of Grahoviste. The civilian inhabitants were taken to other villages and nothing is known of what happened to them. Following this, the Muslims launched an attack on the Pretis munitions factory and a number of Serbs were killed. There was also an incident when 150 cars and a lorry full of shells were misappropriated when Muslim guards were on duty. These events gave rise to a certain distrust and suspicion towards Muslims. The Crisis Staff of Vogosca was established in -- and it operated on democratic principles, issuing guidance to the Assembly Executive Committee. Committees were established for areas including registering abandoned flats, public utilities and shop supplies. As a member of the Crisis Staff, Svetozar Stanic did not receive from any civilian or military authority any orders, instructions, or suggestions concerning the expulsion of non-Serbs from Vogosca. Any Muslims who wanted to leave Vogosca were allowed to do so without any conditions and Muslim residents who remained received the same food supply as Serb residents without any discrimination. Communication between Vogosca and Pale was extremely difficult. A forestry path was used to travel around the villages and to Pale, which was critical as many of the other roads were blocked. Muslims often placed ambushes and -- roadblocks even on this, the only road, and attacked all vehicles travelling on this which were mainly vans carrying wounded to the hospital. Many Serbian civilians had been killed and wounded whilst travelling between Vogosca and Pale. Svetozar Stanic was aware of the Sonja Motel where prisoners of war were temporarily detained until they could be transferred to the Kula prison. Svetozar Stanic also learned about Planjia Kuca prison but only later on from media. While at that time he was in Vogosca he was not aware of this. In relation to the attack on Vogosca SJB, he is aware that it was carried out by Boro Radic of his own accord. Before the outbreak of the war, Radic had led the Patriotic League youth in a parade. When the attack occurred, the police station was still a joint SJB with all nationalities working in it. The situation was resolved without any further loss of lives. However, many people were taken to hospital, where at the same time Juka Prazina was killing in the hospital -- Kosevo Hospital was killing Serbian patients and doctors. Immediately after the event, the BH MUP divided the police forces at all levels. A meeting was organised on 20th of -- around 20th of April, 1992, between members of the SDS, SDA, and the League of Communists of Yugoslavia. Plans formulated by the SDS were suggested for all parties to become involved in the protection of the state, commercial and personal property and public institutions. It was also suggested that the representatives if the -- to these representatives if the SDS and SDA should meet more often and resolve their differences in a peaceful and civilised manner. However, the SDA representatives did not accept the proposal and were inflexible and demanded absolute power of the entire territory of Vogosca municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I have a document that I'd like to ask you about, Mr. Stanic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please call up 1D06726. Could we please have that in e-court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Let's proceed. Do you have any observation, Mr. Tieger?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: With respect to the privacy concerns? I think it's a very good point, Mr. President. I don't know whether it even extends beyond that, but with respect to that level of detail, I certainly agree.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Or if necessary, you can upload a redacted version, redacting only the telephone number later. Let's continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I was [overlapping speakers]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Or probably the address as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. We agree.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Stanic, in this letter is he conveying his regards to other representatives of the authorities through you as well as other prominent Serbs in Vogosca?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR STANIC
utterances.text: Yes. He mentions Jovo Pejovic, a member of the Crisis Staff here, Jovan Pejovic. And also this Beganisic [phoen]. However, he was already in Belgrade by then. I don't know the man, so I did not really get in touch with him. What was his name? Beganisic. As for Jovo Pejovic, who was a member of the Crisis Staff, I told him about that and he was very pleased. He was very pleased to receive such greetings. Your Honours, I have never given anyone this before. It happened to be in my passport when I travelled to Chicago. Chicago, Belgrade, Amsterdam, Chicago, that's how I travelled in 2001, 2002, whatever, so I thought that I could call Mr. Bajrakovic and we could have a cup of coffee, because it wasn't possible then because I was at the airport, only I didn't have a visa for Europe, so I had very little time and we could not really meet up then.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, can I have this marked for identification, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. We'll mark this for identification with the understanding that the redacted version will be uploaded instead of this one. We'll mark it for identification, I mean the redacted one.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 1D6726 receives number D2679, Your Honours, MFI'd.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Just another question, Mr. Stanic. Where did Mr. Bajrakovic live before he left, and how was he enabled to leave?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR STANIC
utterances.text: Mr. Barakovic lived in the urban part of Vogosca, that is to say in the centre basically. Only the basis of a decision of the Crisis Staff of the Municipal Assembly of Vogosca, one of the conclusions was that all people who wished to leave the territory of the municipality of Vogosca, regardless of whether they were Muslims or Croats, that they should be allowed to leave in unhindered fashion with their property, this movable property that they might have had, cars and other movable property.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did the same apply to Serbs, military-aged Serbs?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR STANIC
utterances.text: No. Military-aged Serbs were not allowed, because they had this obligation according to the Law on All National Defence. All Serbs who were called up by the Secretariat of National Defence in the municipality were duty-bound to respond to call-up, and if a person would prove to be able bodied, then they would stay, whereas if people were not capable of doing certain things then they were allowed to leave the municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Stanic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] At this point in time I have no further questions of this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Stanic, as you have noted, your evidence in chief has been admitted in most part in writing in lieu of your oral testimony. Now you'll be cross-examined by the representative of the Office of the Prosecutor, Mr. Tieger. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Good morning, Your Honours. This is actually the first time in days I get to see Judge Baird from this position.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Stanic, as Mr. Karadzic alluded to in his summary, you discuss at paragraph 5 of your statement your views of the instructions of 19 December, otherwise known as variant A and B, including your conclusion regarding its relationship to Bosnian regionalisation six months earlier and that it was a reminder of various laws. Now, in paragraph 8 you also mention the establishment of the Vogosca Crisis Staff on the basis of All People's Defence and social protection. In fact, Mr. Stanic, the Vogosca Crisis Staff, as you indicated in your testimony in the Momcilo Mandic case in 2007, was established in response to the 19 December instructions; correct?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR STANIC
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, I would kindly ask you to deal with these questions one by one. I cannot answer all three questions that you put. So would you agree that we deal with one question first and then the other one, and could we see on the monitor these items that you are interested in?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: By the way, do you have your statement with you now?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My statement is in my jacket. I asked if I could take it with me, and then if not, I could receive a copy from you. So I don't really have it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I think the Court will be happy to provide you with a copy of the statement. And this appears to be a copy here. Now, Mr. Stanic, just to clarify, I referenced paragraph 5 for your benefit but did not ask you a question about it. I referenced paragraph 8 for your benefit but did not ask you a question about it. The question was this: In fact, the Vogosca Crisis Staff was established in response to the 19 December instructions, just as you indicated in your testimony during the Momcilo Mandic case in 2007. That's correct, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR STANIC
utterances.text: Well, let me tell you, I don't remember. In my dossier, or, rather, in my statement it says the Crisis Staff of Vogosca was established on the basis of the Law on All People's Defence and social protection so there were laws and that's how it was established then at the time and we had been cautioned -- or, rather, we were informed that we should invoke the organisation of the Crisis Staff according to this plan A and B. Now, what am I trying to say? I'm trying to say that already in that period there was reason to suspect that Muslims through their representatives in the Assembly of Bosnia-Herzegovina wished to secede by force from -- to have the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina secede and thereby our Serb people too. According to the Law on All People's Defence, a certain caution was given in this way to -- I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I'm sorry to interrupt you, sir, but I'm going to do that when your question -- when your response is not directly -- does not directly answer my question, because I have limited time.

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR STANIC
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: So if I understand your answer correctly, the answer is you were informed, that is, we in Vogosca, I presume, were informed to create the Crisis Staff according to the -- to plan A and B, but then you wanted to explain some of the reasons behind that; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR STANIC
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, I mentioned paragraphs 5 and -- paragraph 5 of your statement in which you focus on various laws and the alleged Bosnian government move towards regionalisation six months earlier, but, Mr. Stanic, the fact is, is it not, that variant A and B provided for the establishment of Serb organs of power. It was about establishing control so that when the war began at that moment in the municipalities where Serbs were in the majority, they had municipal power, held it firmly, controlled everything, and in the municipalities where they were in the minority, they had set up secret government, Municipal Boards, Assemblies, that they had set up a government and a brigade, a unit, no matter what size, and there was a detachment with a commander? That's the thrust of what A and B was about and what it accomplished; correct?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR STANIC
utterances.text: That is not very precise. I have to refer you to certain legal provisions in relation to plan A and B. I said then also and in my statement that this is based in -- on the Law of the All People's Defence of the former Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina if it is in accordance with the then SFRY, that is to say the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia. So the Crisis Staffs were established in municipalities, even in local communes. The Crisis Staff of Vogosca had --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Stanic, excuse me. All right. Are you -- again and I want to focus on the question. These are not platforms for you to explain everything you might want to say about the general topic, so just please try to focus on the question and we will move, I think, in a more logical fashion. So with respect to what I described to you, you said that is not very precise. Does that mean you think there are other aspects that could be elaborated on including what you consider to be the underlying legal basis, or does that mean you're saying that's not wrong and that I was not providing an accurate summary?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR STANIC
utterances.text: Well, you didn't provide an accurate summary, sir, because, and this is why I wanted to point this out, to explain this to avoid any mistakes so that you don't have an impression that it could be interpreted in various ways, my interpretation is that all the municipalities in Bosnia-Herzegovina at the time had in accordance with the law the right to form Crisis Staffs if there was an imminent threat of war, an external or internal threat. The Serbian part of Vogosca municipality, well, there was also a Muslim part in Kobilja Glava, they had their Crisis Staffs before we did --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] Mr. Stanic, stop, please. I'm sorry, sir. And I know it feels [overlapping speakers]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. Just a second. Let's hear him out this time.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. President, that's -- that's -- I'm always willing to do so but I've been given extremely limited time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We'll bear that in mind.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Let's proceed. Okay. You were stopped when you were saying, "a Muslim part in Kobilja Glava, they had their Crisis Staff before we did." Please continue.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] They had a Crisis Staff before we did, and throughout Bosnia and Herzegovina the Muslims and the HDZ had their own Crisis Staffs. So we established our Crisis Staff in the municipality of Vogosca in January or February 1992, whereas the HDZ established its Crisis Staffs sometime in September 1991. The SDA, the Muslim Party of Democratic Action, established its Crisis Staffs even before the multi-party elections held in November 1990, and these were paramilitary formations, the Patriotic League and the Green Berets and Lilies, and so on and so forth. So they already had their Crisis Staffs that were legally maintained. We were aware of their existence and this was a response to that. We Serbs who at the time felt under threat thought we had to organise ourselves as best we could in order to protect ourselves and all the others living in the area regardless of their ethnicity, their nationality. We wanted to be secure in those areas and this was above all a means of procuring food, providing health care, treatment, and everything else. I can't remember all the details, but everything else in accordance with the Law of All People's Protection and social self protection.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Two things quickly. First of all, Mr. Stanic, can you tell me where, that is, what provision of the SFRY Law on All people's Defence uses the term "Crisis Staff"?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR STANIC
utterances.text: Well, the Crisis Staff -- well, it's in accordance with the constitution, with the laws in force in Socialist Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina at the time. As for the article concerned, I can't remember them now. If I had prepared this, I'd be able to refer to these articles that addressed this issue, but I can't tell you that according to those provisions on All People's Defence, its well-known Law on All People's Defence and self protection, according to this law which is based on the constitution of the SFRY, well, these constitutions are in accordance with the republican constitutions, so that is the situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: All right. So you can't tell me that and in fact I put it to you, Mr. Stanic, that there is no mention of Crisis Staff in the SFRY Law on All People's Defence at all.

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR STANIC
utterances.text: As far as I know it is mentioned, the Crisis Staffs in certain situations, and this also concerns republican ones. I can tell you that president of the Territorial Defence at the time was Franjo Herljevic, and he was also the president of the civilian protection, and Crisis Staffs also were considered to be Crisis Staffs in certain segments for certain units, for certain republican levels, but the republics would then transfer this to municipal levels to Municipal Boards.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: All right. I'm also going to put it to you that it's not mentioned in the constitution, but I want to talk to you about what the -- what I raised earlier, and that is that irrespective of the legal provisions you mentioned, the answer you gave had nothing to do with whether or not when the war began in the municipalities where the Serbs were in the majority they had municipal power, held it firmly, controlled everything, and in the municipalities where they were in the minority set up secret government, et cetera, and in any event had a government and a brigade. That -- what I read to you earlier, that you said was not precise, Mr. Stanic, that you said was not accurate, those were not my words, Mr. Stanic. Those were the words of Mr. Karadzic to the Bosnian Serb Assembly in April of 1995.

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR STANIC
