utterances.text: In April 1995. I don't know what Mr. Karadzic said then, but all I can do is give another explanation. In the territory where the authorities were mixed, the Serbs and Muslims, I'm talking about the municipality of Vogosca, there the local communes in accordance with the law concerning the organisation, they could leave certain municipalities if they weren't happy. This was in accordance with the Law on Constitution, Article 263 or 235 of the constitution of Bosnia and Herzegovina, and they could join up with another municipality or establish a new municipality. And it is on the basis of those laws, if I may continue --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: No, you may not continue. I'm asking you, please, about variant A and B. I'm not asking you about other legal bases that in your view would have permitted the municipalities to take certain action. I'm asking you about this particular document, why it was disseminated, and how it was implemented. Now, I just cited you language about what A and B accomplished. You said it was wrong, and now I turned your attention to the fact that it was Dr. Karadzic who said that. Now, do you still dispute that that was the effect of variant A and B?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR STANIC
utterances.text: Well, variants A and B are defined in that way. May I comment on them so that we get the right answer?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I don't want a dissertation on A and B generally. I want an answer to my question. Do you still dispute that that -- it is wrong to say that was the effect of variant A and B, that that's what it accomplished? You had a full opportunity to describe your other views about A and B in your statement. Now I'm asking you about very precise aspects of it.

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR STANIC
utterances.text: Could you put that direct question to me once more, please, if it's not too difficult.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I asked you if it wasn't the case that A and B provided for the establishment of Serb organs of power and was about establishing control over territories so that at the moment the war began in the municipality where the Bosnian Serbs were in the majority they had municipal power, held it firmly, controlled everything. In the municipalities where they were in the minority they set up secret government, Municipal Boards, Municipal Assemblies, presidents of Executive Boards. You will remember the A and B variant. In the B variant where we're in the minority, we had set up a government brigade --

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR STANIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes. Yes. We established that at the time, but it's not a secret. It was done quite publicly.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. And in Vogosca, it was Jovan Tintor who -- who became the president of the Crisis Staff, who created military formations, a brigade, indeed went from municipality to municipality creating military formations on order from his president; correct?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR STANIC
utterances.text: No. Jovan Tintor was the president of the Crisis Staff of Vogosca. As a member of the Main Board of the SDS of Bosnia and Herzegovina, and therefore he did not organise those military brigades. On the contrary, the Crisis Staff issued instructions to executive committee of the Municipal Assembly. They were to carry out a mobilisation, and it was the secretary for national defence of the Municipal Assembly of Vogosca, Jovan Pradanovic [phoen], who was responsible for this, and he called up all members who wanted to respond to the call-up in accordance with the law, all members who wanted to respond to this mobilisation.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Tintor, in fact, was the head of the illegal brigade in Vogosca. Isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR STANIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well again, Mr. Stanic, I'm quoting the words of Mr. Karadzic before the Bosnian Serb Assembly: "We made various calculations and agreements with Yugoslavia. We decided to set up the TO, the Serbian brigades, which were indeed led by the SDS but not as a party army but as people's army, for not everyone dared to put himself at the head of an illegal brigade and oppose the Green Berets like Jovan Tintor." And that's at P00970. That's what Dr. Karadzic said about Jovan Tintor in front of the Assembly and in front of Mr. Tintor. Do you still dispute that?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters are kindly asking the counsel not to touch his microphone while talking.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] President of the Crisis Staff, and in the Crisis Staff at the time, at the beginning, there were 21 members as far as I can remember, and the Crisis Staff issued guidelines to the Executive Committee, Executive Board of the Municipal Assembly of Vogosca, and before the war the president of the Municipal Assembly was Rajko Kopravica, and don't want -- Mr. Karadzic said about Jovan Tintor, but while I was there Jovo Peranovic was Secretary of National Defence established, or, rather, issued a call-up for mobilisation. All the reserve officers responded all those who had served in the JNA or were serving in the JNA and it was their responsibility to respond to the call-up in accordance with the law. At the time in accordance with those regulations a brigade was established in Vogosca in the neighbourhood where Captain Zoric, reserve captain, was. He -- deceased. The brigade was established in Blagovac and Miladin Trifunovic was the commander there. So those are the brigades that were established on the basis of the call-up issued by the municipal authorities, Krivoglavci, Semizovac, all those who responded at the time became part of those brigades.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I quoted you earlier from Mr. Karadzic describing variant A and B and what he continued to say at that time was about the SDS organising the people and creating the army. Was that -- that army that had been created by the SDS together with the police were the armed forces of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, "They created the space, liberated and created the space." And again that's found at P970. You'll find that at English pages 316 through 317. Now, Mr. Stanic, the space that was liberated by the Bosnian Serb forces was sometimes in areas where the Bosnian Serbs were a majority and sometimes in areas where the Muslims were a majority but that there were strategic or other reasons, economic, for example, for the Bosnian Serbs to seek that territory; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR STANIC
utterances.text: Sir, could you please put questions to me about the Vogosca Municipal Assembly. Don't ask me questions of a general kind. The Vogosca Municipal Assembly established its units in the territory where the Serbs were in the majority. That's Krivoglavci - I mentioned that place earlier - Blagovac as well, Vogosca, or the urban part of Vogosca, Donji Vogosca, Semizovci, and so on and so forth. So those are places where the Serbs were locals. They had been so for centuries. And according to the last election they were in the majority. I can answer such questions but don't ask me about these general issues as to who lived where. I had so many problems at the -- at that time that I was concerned with these problems that I'm testifying about here today.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Try to focus on the question and not elaborate more than is necessary. I'll ask you about Vogosca first of all.

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR STANIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: According to the 1991 census, Vogosca was a Muslim majority municipality. There were more Muslims in Vogosca than Serbs; correct?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR STANIC
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And in Vogosca, it was the view of the political leadership from the beginning that Vogosca had to be taken because of its industry. That's correct also, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR STANIC
utterances.text: Vogosca, well, that's partially correct. What is fully correct is the following: Pretis and Vogosca, the urban part was 70 per cent Serb. Pretis, Utava [phoen], Tasa [phoen], Vogosca, that area, that urban area had a majority of Serbs in comparison to Vukovlja [phoen] Glava, Hotonj, Barice where that wasn't the case. So therefore we didn't conquer anything. We didn't take any territory. We protected the military industry, economic facilities in Vogosca at the time and at the time Vogosca was one of the strongest municipalities in the Socialist Federative Republic of Yugoslavia. There was the Pretis industry there, one of the largest place in the Balkans. There was a bed factory Tas and Unis, and there was the Tas car factory where Volkswagens were produced, or, rather, 50 per cent of it was Tas. So that was industry that was of importance and Pretis is a military industry --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Stanic, I fear it's not going to be possible to educate you on your full tendency to elaborate on everything that's raised, but now you're giving me a dissertation on the full extent of industry in Vogosca which hasn't been asked for. So let me return to the subject we were discussing and that was the reason to take Vogosca.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And in that connection may I call up P05511.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And I'm going to direct your attention to a meeting of the Vogosca Serbian Municipal Assembly held on the 14th of November, 1992, which was attended by, among other people, yourself. In fact, it appeared that as president of the Serbian Municipal Assembly, you chaired the meeting. And by Mr. Momcilo Krajisnik. And if we turn to page 3 of the English and page 5 of the B/C/S we see Mr. -- a reflection of Mr. Krajisnik's remarks. And in the middle of the page in English it states the opinion of the political leadership about Vogosca is positive. In the beginning the opinion was take Vogosca because of its industry. That's correct, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR STANIC
utterances.text: No, that's not correct. We didn't take the industry in Vogosca. We protected it, because this was the property of the Secretariat for National Defence in the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, and this is Pretis, and according to those directives we protected it. We didn't take it, because the attack on the 17th and 18th of April took place on Vogosca. And it was the Muslim forces who went from Hotonj, Barice, Kobilja Glava, Sarajevo. There were paramilitary units and they took it on that occasion and then the JNA got involved. So Pretis was the property of the SSNO. We did not take it. We just protected it. And I also asked the Muslim side at a meeting to protect --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers]

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR STANIC
utterances.text: -- it. I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I'm sure you'll get better at this. By that time, that is the 14th of November, 1992, in fact the Bosnian Serbs had taken 80 per cent of Vogosca and were still looking to -- looking for more, that is looking to liberate, in their words, more. That's correct, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR STANIC
utterances.text: Vogosca. I don't know which period you are referring to now, sir, but --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Let me look at the remarks of Miladin T. I presume that's Mr. Trifunovic. That's page 2 of the English, also page 2 of the B/C/S. He says, We took -- this is toward the top of the page in English. We took 80 per cent out of 30 per cent of the territories. And then he goes on in the next long paragraph, we have to clean up the area of the Kobilja Glava, et cetera, et cetera, we will finish our job and liberate it. Now, there Mr. Trifunovic is talking about the extent of Vogosca territory that has been taken up to that point and about the intention to take more; correct?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR STANIC
utterances.text: That's not correct. That is not correct for the simple reason that at the Vogosca Municipal Assembly, there were -- in the Municipal Assembly there were several local communities, and wherever the Muslims were in the majority we didn't tamper with them. We didn't agree on anything. On the contrary, at one of the meetings of the Crisis Staff Miladin Trifunovic was issued a task as the commander of the Blagovac Battalion. Since Blagovac was above battalion, his task was to protect Pretis and to make sure no one damaged it. And his second task was that Mr. Miladin Trifunovic should communicate with the Tihovici local commune which was a neighbouring local commune and nothing was to be done to provoke a conflict or incident of any kind. So that was his task issued by the Crisis Staff. I can tell you that and I can stand by that. And on the other hand, Uglasuglevci [phoen] was never attacked Ugorsko, Ugljesici, Betanija, and Kobilja Glava --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Now, go ahead. You were dealing with Kobilja Glava, please, and that's what I wanted to direct your attention to. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR STANIC
utterances.text: So at that time we did not take or conquer anything. All we did was protect our local communes. This was done in agreement with the presidents of the local communities and in agreement with the deputies, representatives. These were the local communities where the Serbs were in the majority. So there was an exceptional case around the beginning of May. If I may, sir, explain this.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: No, please, unless the Court wants you to --

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR STANIC
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I want to focus on this. So do I understand that you're telling -- do I understand correctly that you're telling this Court that when Mr. Trifunovic said on May -- on November 14th that they were not satisfied with the amount of territory and spoke about plans to finish the job and liberate Kobilja Glava, that that was not correct, that there were no plans to liberate Kobilja Glava?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR STANIC
utterances.text: I can claim with full responsibility that I don't know about this, and there were no discussions about taking Kobilja Glava, Tihonje [phoen] or Barice. I can claim this with full responsibility, and I don't know what he was saying at the Assembly. I can't remember. But you know, this is the truth. I'm telling you this with full responsibility, and I stand by everything I said.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, then let's turn to a meeting of the very next day, the 15th of November, 1992. And this was a meeting of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps command, which was attended by various members of the command and also various officials from Sarajevo municipalities, including Mr. Prstojevic, from Ilidza; Mr. Radic, Trifko Radic, president of the Sarajevo Assembly; and yourself, the president of Vogosca municipality. And if we turn to page 16 of the English and page 11 of the B/C/S, we see remarks by you, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Do you have the exhibit number or the 65 ter number.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: My apologies, Mr. President. Yes, it's P5065.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And there we see your remarks. You greet the audience and then speak of "the five municipalities to create plans with the commanders to liberate Kobilja Glava." So despite your assertion that you can claim to this Court with full responsibility that there were no plans to liberate Kobilja Glava, the precise opposite was true, Mr. Stanic?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR STANIC
utterances.text: Can I see who signed the minutes and who kept it, because I don't recognise this. I don't recognise myself in these words.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Stanic, you can look at the front page of the document. You can look over the entire document, as far as I'm concerned, if you want.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Shall we show the first page -- just a second --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Perhaps just the first page.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And for your information, the record was taken by Colonel Aleksa Krsmanovic, and that's indicated at the end of the document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. Last page.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Public Prosecutor, believe me when I say that I met Aleksa Krsmanovic for the first time in Belgrade when he was released. I believe he had been taken prisoner by the Muslim forces together with General Djukic. That is when I met him for the first time, Mr. Krsmanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: There were a lot of people at this meeting, obviously, Mr. Stanic. I'm not suggesting you met him at a formal introduction to him at the meeting. He's the note-taker at that meeting taking elaborate notes on a very long meeting in great detail and indicating your presence very clearly, giving your titled, where you're from, and recording what you said.

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR STANIC
utterances.text: I wasn't able to see where the meeting was held. If possible, could we go back to that page?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Beginning of the document indicates pursuant an order of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps command, consultations --

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR STANIC
utterances.text: Command of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Consultation was held at the Slobodan P. Zelja barracks in Lukavica beginning at 10.00 and ending at 16.30 on the 15th of November, 1992.

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR STANIC
utterances.text: I state responsibly that I was not present at that meeting. As far as I know, the Municipal Assembly of Vogosca municipality lasted a long time, the session of the 14th of November, 1992. It was then when I resigned. Following my resignation, I no longer took part in any activities. That is why I'm saying this. That is why I do not recall this. I told you when I saw Mr. Krsmanovic for the first time and it was the only time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: But do you see your name, Mr. Stanic, on number 20 -- 20 --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I see it. I see it. I saw it before. But I'm telling you that I wasn't present at the meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I just want to clarify one more thing with respect to Kobilja Glava. That was a settlement or a village or area consisting of 2.866 people, 2.750 of whom were Muslims, four of whom were Croats, and 46 Serbs, along with 37 Yugoslavs. Is that correct or approximately correct, Mr. Stanic?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR STANIC
utterances.text: I was moving the headset or the microphone, so I couldn't hear you well. If possible, could you please repeat the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Sure I just wanted you to confirm the demographics of Kobilja Glava as indicated in 1991 census and that would be approximately 2.866 people, about 2.750 of whom were Muslim.

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR STANIC
utterances.text: I think so. I don't see wrong with the figures. I don't know precisely, but I presume it was as you put.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Stanic, you were asked in -- about detention facilities in Vogosca, and that's reflected in paragraph 13 of your statement, and you emphasise that your responsibilities on the Crisis Staff were related to commercial matters and noted that someone else was, and that's Mr. Luketa, I believe, was in charge of matters related to detention facilities. So as I understand it, you assert that your information about such facilities was limited because that was not your job.

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR STANIC
utterances.text: That's right. But I wasn't in charge of commercial matters, but I was in charge of legal and trade entities in Vogosca municipality, and I was tasked to conduct negotiations with the SDA and HDZ representatives. I was tasked to do that by my party if such talks ever occurred at the -- on the local level.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Now, you did mention that you knew about the existence of Sonja's place, and I wanted to ask you whether you knew that it was established by the Crisis Staff.

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR STANIC
utterances.text: Yes. The Crisis Staff established Sonja's as a place where people could be interrogated, and that was also the first headquarters of the Crisis Staff once we left the adult education centre. We moved to the Sonja Motel then, and at one of the sessions the Crisis Staff decided to take over the facility from Zeljko Beganovic. He happened to have been a good friend of mine together with his mother Sonja because I used to take lunch there often, and that's where the Crisis Staff was set up. After some shellings from Ugljesici and Ugarsko we had to move the Crisis Staff and we actually changed location every three or four sessions because we were in danger. A decision was made by the Crisis Staff to set up an interrogation and judicial facility at the motel in order to be able to conduct investigations of prisoners so that they could be sent onward to Kula or processed further. That's the truth of it. Perhaps I elaborated a bit.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Now, do I understand, then, that you were not familiar with a detention facility called the bunker, which was close to Sonja's place?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR STANIC
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, since I grew up in that part of Vogosca, I can tell you the bunker facility dates back to World War II. I recall it. It is some 200 metres away, although I never went there, so I don't know precisely. In any case, when I was a young man and I went to swim there, it had always been locked.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Sorry. I should have asked that a bit more precisely, and that is were you familiar with the use of the bunker as a detention facility?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR STANIC
utterances.text: No. I didn't know that, and I explained that there was a metal door at the entrance of the bunker. I remember it since when I was a little boy on my way to swim. It was overgrown, and I never actually saw it with my own eyes. I have never heard that it was used as a kind of prison or anything else.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: You've indicated you never heard that it was used as a prison or anything else. Let me just get a little more clarity on this. Are you claiming that you know that it was not used as a facility or that you just never heard that it was and you don't know whether or not it was or was not?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR STANIC
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, I never heard of such intentions, and I have no knowledge that it was used to that end. I only know of the Sonja's place as a location designated by the Crisis Staff. Now, what was done there, who brought whom, and whether they used the bunker, that's something I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, there's a man by the name of Slobodan Avlijas who is on the Defence witness list who was an assistant minister of justice in 1992, and he testified at the trial of Momcilo Mandic that he came to Vogosca, saw the bunker and that the conditions were "truly horrific." Indeed, he said that when he was talking about it many, many years later, he was "still horrified." Do you have any reason to doubt that, that is that he observed the bunker was being used as a detention facility and that conditions were horrific?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR STANIC
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, really, I never received such information from him. If he came there, I guess he should have turned to those competent in the Municipal Assembly of Vogosca municipality and the Executive Council as well as to the administrative and judicial bodies. If I had known about it, although I had no power in the Executive Board, being its president, I would have insisted to shut it down. I didn't know. That's what I can repeat. And I'm not familiar with it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Avlijas testified at the Mandic trial not only that he was horrified by the conditions of the bunker but also that he met with Mr. Koprivica, the chairman of the Executive Board, Mr. Zdravko Luketa who was in charge of these matters as I believe you indicated for the Crisis Staff, and yourself, and complained about those "truly horrific" conditions at the bunker.

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR STANIC
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, I can only repeat what I've just said. I wasn't aware of it, and that he did not talk to me on that topic. I assert that.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we have the date of Avlijas's visit?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I can call up the 65 ter number if -- well, that's a little bit much for a witness on Mr. Karadzic's own list. I'm reciting fully accurately what Mr. Avlijas testified to in the Mandic trial.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Let us proceed, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just for planning purpose how much longer would you need, Mr. Tieger?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Here's what I have to discuss with the witness left,

utterances.speaker: MR. PRESIDENT
utterances.text: I want to discuss the status of the detainees as reflected in several documents related to the Crisis Staff, and then I want to discuss with him the issue of volunteers. So I would imagine that's -- given how time has gone thus far, I would imagine about 20 minutes unless the length of the answers changes abruptly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: If you could try to conclude before the break.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I'm doing my absolute best, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Okay. I want to discuss with you, Mr. Stanic, how the detainees at the bunker and other facilities got there. First of all -- and who they were, okay? Now, I understand you testified at the -- at the Mandic case that you didn't have information about civilians being taken prisoner, that you referred to prisoners of war. Do you recall that testimony or -- or not?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR STANIC
utterances.text: I recall my testimony.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Okay. Are you saying that you know for a fact that civilians were never detained and held in detention facilities in Vogosca or -- or just that you didn't have information to that effect, which of the two?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR STANIC
utterances.text: The only one is that the -- that I know of some detainees in the Sonja's facility. That's what I know about and I stand by it. I can repeat. On one occasion Zdravko Luketa, a judge, called me to visit it. We were preparing to do so but I was called to an urgent meeting in Ilidza and I didn't accompany him to the facility.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Are you aware that Crisis Staff documentation distinguished between persons who were considered prisoners of war and persons who were not, that is, the nature of the documentation indicated that some were prisoners of war and some wrote not?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR STANIC
utterances.text: As far as I recall, of course there were -- there were POWs and detainees who were first placed in the Sonja Motel. They were interrogated there, and if they had to be processed further or serve their sentences, they were sent on to the Kula facility because we had no such conditions to keep them. And Mr. Zdravko Luketa, who passed away in the meantime and who was then the court president, told me the same thing on a number of occasions.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: In respect of my earlier question I want to show you three documents. The first is 65 ter 24003. This is a document signed by Mr. Koprivica, and it orders as follows: You are hereby ordered to set free the Muslim prisoner of war. It provides his name, and it indicates that he used to be exchanged for Mr. Colic, who is a member of the VRS and that that order shall come into effect immediately. The next document is 24088. This is a document --

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR STANIC
utterances.text: Do I need to comment on this?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I'll ask you a question. These two documents are related, as you'll see, and I'll ask you a question about those in a moment.

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR STANIC
utterances.text: This is a document of the 29th of July, 1992, again signed by Mr. Koprivica, and it orders the release of the following Muslim prisoners of war is hereby ordered. It names these two. It indicates that they are to be handed over to the commission for the exchange of prisoners and the order is effective immediately. Now, I showed you those documents, Mr. Stanic, so -- and I wanted to ask you if we can agree that the Crisis Staff, when it was capable of and in fact did identify someone as someone they considered to be a prisoner of war, explicitly when they considered that to be the case.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please see where this refers to the War Staff?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is the War Commission.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] followed on the heels of the Crisis Staff?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR STANIC
utterances.text: So it's got nothing to do with the Crisis Staff, Mr. Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Let me ask you another way. The officials, the authorities of Vogosca in charge of such matters, that is -- and in this case the commission which took over after on -- in -- in -- which was the official body following the Crisis Staff was fully capable of indicating who in their case -- who in their view they considered to be a prisoner of war and did so explicitly in their documentation.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the witness be -- could the witness receive another interpretation of the question slowly so that he understand it well. I don't think the interpretation of the question was accurate. Could we have another interpretation of the question while we wait?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: For what it's worth it's a little unusual for me for counsel to be asking for -- on behalf of a witness to be taking the position that the witness doesn't understand a question. The witness is fully capable of letting us know if he don't understand the question or not. Now, I'll repeat it, Mr. Stanic, if you wish.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. Could you repeat your question, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: The officials in Vogosca in charge of the detention and release of prisoners, in this case the War Commission, were fully capable of indicating who in their view they considered to be a prisoner of war and of explicitly indicating that view in the documentation connected with the release or exchange of such detainees.

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR STANIC
utterances.text: First of all, let me explain something right away. Mr. President was right that this was not a matter of the Crisis Staff, but this was the War Commission which was set up on the 1st of June, 1992. As for this order, I cannot comment on it, because it was part of the remit of the Executive Board of the Municipal Assembly and of the judiciary. I don't know where these prisoners were being held or, as they are referred to, prisoners of war. I've never heard of them. I don't know whether they were placed somewhere temporarily in Vogosca or whether they were serving their sentence at the Kula facility. I cannot give you a precise answer, because I'm unaware of it all as a member -- as for me being a member of the War Commission, well, I wasn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Yeah, you said that - it's in your statement - and, Mr. Stanic, as well as your surprise that you, as an official at that level, didn't transition into the War Commission like other officials; correct?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR STANIC
utterances.text: It's not clear to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: You were surprised that you as the president of the municipality didn't transition from the Crisis Staff into the War Commission as the other -- as most of the other officials of that level did; correct? And you express that surprise in your statement.

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR STANIC
utterances.text: It is correct that I was not a member of the War Commission. It is also correct that I held such functions and positions as tasked by the War Commission. It was an operational team comprising five people. When invited by the president of that commission, I attended certain meetings of theirs, only a number of them, but I wasn't familiar with this topic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: All right. And I want to look at P2367. This is a document related to the exchange of prisoners on the 25th of May, 1992. And this does concern the Crisis Staff prior to the transition from Crisis Staff into War Commission. Now, this relates to the release from detention on condition of exchange of certain persons who are listed both in that first page of the document and then on a couple of handwritten appended pages, and it describes them as follows: "The citizens of Muslim ethnicity captured during fighting in the residential area of Svrake will be released from detention ...," et cetera. Now, Mr. Stanic can we agree that that language the citizen of Muslim ethnicity captured in residential area, et cetera, is a reference to the fact that these people are civilians, not prisoners of war?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: Where does it say civilian? In a civil war, citizens fight --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger is putting his question to the witness. It's for the witness to answer the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. President, if I may, that is really a patently inappropriate intervention.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But I don't know -- I don't know if it is allowed to introduce such words without the exact word "civilian" being mentioned in the document. In our system --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] And it -- and it -- and it persists.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, you are feeding the answer to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers]

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, I'm only asking Mr. Tieger to show us where it says civilian.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Do not overlap, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Mr. President, but as the Court has observed before once the intervention take place the objection is -- is no longer has any point.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Excellencies, may I explain?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, the Chamber finds your intervention this time very improper and inappropriate. In the future, if you'd like to make an observation, could you tell us just you have an objection without putting the question. Then the Chamber will see whether we need to hear your submission in the absence of the witness or not. And this time we'll not -- we don't have to hear you further. We agree with Mr. Tieger that his -- his question is fair enough, in the Chamber's view. Would you like take a break, Mr. Tieger, or you can conclude in five minutes?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I think it's better probably to take a break, Mr. President, and I will absolutely pare down the remaining questions to the bare minimum. I will try to conclude in -- as quickly as possible. There won't be much time afterwards, but I'll do my best to make it even less than what it would have been.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We will take a break for 45 minutes and resume at quarter past 1.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Tieger, please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Stanic, I want to complete our discussion of this document and then move on to very briefly discuss our remaining topic. Looking at P2367, the document of 25 May 1992, issued by the head of the department for judiciary administration and regulations with the consent of the Crisis Staff, the language used there, Mr. Stanic, to refer to those persons held, that is citizens of Muslim ethnicity, the reference to their capture in the residential area of Svrake, that language in contrast to the explicit denotations we saw in the previous two documents that you looked at is a reflection of the understanding that these people were civilians. Isn't that right, Mr. Stanic?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR STANIC
utterances.text: No. These are members of the army -- or, rather, the Patriotic League, and if I may, Mr. Prosecutor, I would like to give a deeper or broader explanation in order for you to get an impression as to who this was. During or, rather, before the outbreak of the war --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Stanic, if this is something that Mr. Karadzic cares to get into, he's welcome to do so, but I understand that your answer is that when this document referred to the citizens of Muslim ethnicity and describes where they were captured, that your view -- your position is that is a way to refer to people who were considered to be POWs; correct?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, did he not say that he believed -- or they were members of the Patriotic League, and he was cut off while giving the reason for his -- for his -- such impression or belief. Mr. Stanic, could you continue.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As I started to say a moment ago, these are members of paramilitary units or, rather, the Patriotic League that was established even before the multi-party elections were held in November 1990. The task of these paramilitary units was as follows: From well-founded sources we learned that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Stopping there, but what is your basis? What was your basis for such a conclusion that they were the members of the paramilitary unit?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I told you that I had to give a deeper explanation. On the basis of sources, a certain Nenad Spiric, who secretly got into the Svrake local commune, ethnically that's about 95 per cent, 96 per cent Muslim populated, it's a village, these are only privately owned housed, there aren't any urban facilities there, he hid there, the rascal, and he saw all their plans and all their agreements as to what should be done. To tell you the truth, at first I didn't believe that, but the Crisis Staff made a decision, namely that in the barracks opposite Svrake certain posts should be filled. There was a captain there who was a Montenegrin and a Macedonian who was, I don't know what, a sergeant, and the members of the Territorial Defence entered there to safeguard the property of the JNA. From Svrake. And then later on I found out --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Stanic, please concentrate on answering the question. So take a look at this list. I take it you can read the first -- first three or four names. On what basis that you are saying that Camil Cehajic was a member of the paramilitary?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, that's what I wanted to explain to you, that paramilitary units are actually the Patriotic League. They were paramilitary units at the time, because the MUP was still in existence, and even before that there was the Yugoslav People's Army, the JNA. Now, we had to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. -- could you read out the name after Camil Cehajic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, to tell you I can read this in the English version. In my version to tell you the truth, you can't really see it. I don't even know these names. And that's why they were detained, to see who it was that they were, actually, so that we could see whether they were members of the paramilitary units and whether they were residents of the local commune of Svrake, because they had surrendered after a while. That was --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Stanic, my question is the second name reads as Alija Halilovic. How do you know he was a member of Patriotic League?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, Judge, Your Honour, Mr. President, that is why we had to examine this. That is why this list was in the Crisis Staff and in the secretariat for justice, to look into the matter to see whether they were Patriotic League or not. If they were not, then they were exchanged for Serb prisoners, and that was the decision of the judiciary organs of the Municipal Assembly of Vogosca.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And if they were, what would happen to them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If they were, then they would be dealt with at the Kula prison and where their intentions and tasks would be looked at. I don't know any of these names. And the Crisis Staff didn't know either.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And you said if they were not, then they were exchanged for Serb prisoners. Then do you agree then those prisoners who were not members of Patriotic League were civilians?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, they were not civilians. All of them were military conscripts. All of them were young-ish men. So they were not civilians. All of them carried weapons. Now, within this agreement, certain exchanges were supposed to take place, and they all took part in the attack against the JNA barracks in Semizovac. We could not make a distinction as to who members of the Patriotic League were and who were the people who were planted there by the MUP of Bosnia-Herzegovina illegally to take the barracks of the JNA and to cut off the road between Visoko and Sarajevo. For that reason this had to be looked into to see who they were, what they were doing and how many people were planted there from the MUP who had special tasks of their own.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Back to you, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I move on to the volunteers. I'd also like to tender the previous two documents we looked at, 24003 and 24088.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: What was the document that bears 24088?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: The 29 July release to [indiscernible] of war.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: They were shown in quick succession.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic do you have any objection to the admission of 24003? Vogosca War Commission document.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, if I were to see it I believe I wouldn't have any objections, but now I can no longer tell which document it is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Shall we upload it, 24003. Two prisoners of war to be handed over to the War Commission.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. No objection. I believe the document is authentic, although this witness perhaps didn't know this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Given the accused's position, we will receive this.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 24003 receives number P6058, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And shall we upload the next document.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No objection, your Excellency.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 24088 receives Exhibit P6059, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Stanic, in paragraph 14 of your statement --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just one clarification. In para 13 of -- of the witness's statement, he refers to so-called Planina Kuca. Does it mean bunker?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: No. It's a reference to -- I believe that's a -- I mean, as the witness, of course. But I think Kuca is home, house

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] Where do you have bunker in his statement?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: He doesn't reference the bunker in the statement, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So you asked about it for the first time.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Stanic, in paragraph 14 of your statement you state what you know about the volunteers, As it begins in connection with the volunteers I know the following, and you explain that a group of volunteers led by Jovo Ostojic arrived and were immediately placed under the command of the VRS and who sent them. Now, Mr. Stanic, what you didn't mention is the fact that the municipality paid the volunteers. That's correct, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR STANIC
utterances.text: What do you mean the municipality paid them, the volunteers?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR STANIC
utterances.text: Again, I will have to give a lengthier explanation. According to the Law on All People's Defence, the status of volunteers is defined. So a volunteer is every person who does not have a wartime assignment and who wishes to volunteer of their own free will into an armed unit. So the duties and responsibilities of volunteers are defined in the Law on All People's Defence. So the municipality is not duty-bound. This goes through the ministry. And now it depends which one, how this was financed. So volunteers and military conscripts in regular armed forces of Republika Srpska have the same obligations.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Okay. As before, you provided a -- some sort of legal dissertation on the status of the subject matter. My question, I think, is a bit simpler, and that is: Did Vogosca authorities provide payment to the volunteers or seek payment for funds to go to the volunteers? Was that something that the municipal authorities of Vogosca did that was, in fact, not mentioned in paragraph 14 of your statement?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR STANIC
utterances.text: It is not mentioned in paragraph 14 of my statement. That's true. It's right here in front of me. But it's possible that they did pay, the municipal authorities did, but with the possibility of being refunded from the Ministry of Defence of Republika Srpska, the appropriate organs. It's possible, but I cannot recall. It's been a long time after all.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Let's look at P2373. This is a document dated the 15th of July, 1992. It's a document sent by you and signed by you, sent to the Ministry of Finance seeking reimbursement of funds, including reimbursement of funds in the name of reimbursements to volunteers. In the English by the way there's a tiny typo. It seems to say 500. As we can see in the B/C/S, it actually says 500.000. This document, Mr. Stanic, is a reflection of the fact that the municipal authorities were funding the volunteers and then later seeking reimbursement, in this instance from the republic authorities of RS.

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR STANIC
utterances.text: That's right. The date is the 15th of July, as we see, and then the municipal secretary, that is to say the secretary for national defence of the Municipal Assembly of Vogosca, he wrote this up, and I signed it technically. Why did I do that? It was only the president of the municipality that could sign a document and have the stamp affixed there. I do not doubt this, that this was my signature, and this is correct information, because the secretary for national defence of the Municipal Assembly of Vogosca had a list and he knew exactly who should get what and these resources should get refunded. So you can see this and this is quite all right, and, as I said a moment ago, they have these rights and responsibilities like all other members of the armed forces and volunteers.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Now, in addition to the fact that the municipality funded the volunteers, what is also left out of paragraph 14 when you describe what you know about the volunteers is the fact that officials from Vogosca went to get them, and, in fact, Mr. Stanisic you went to get them; correct?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR STANIC
utterances.text: That's correct. I went there because this was a case of volunteers from Sombor, and this is the association of Serbs from Bosnia-Herzegovina in the territory of Serbia and they had a section of their own in Sombor, and these young men volunteered saying that they wanted to join up because originally they hailed from Bosnia-Herzegovina. The parents during the 1940s, they were transferred to Vojvodina, Srem, Backa, Baranja. That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I have nothing further for this witness, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Tieger. Mr. Karadzic, do you have any re-examination?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do, Excellency, a bit more than usual.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Stanic, as for these papers A and B that you were asked about, did you take this to be an instruction or a binding order to act?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR STANIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, this was an instruction that we had received in order to analyse it, and this is what I can tell you: When we received this instruction as to how we should behave, there was this legal team of the Municipal Assembly of Vogosca that worked on this and compared it to appropriate legal provisions and we thought that this was in accordance with Law on National Defence and social self protection and that is why I referred to all of that in my letter.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In which situations are ad hoc bodies created in our part of the world? Regardless whether they're called Crisis Staffs or War Presidency in which are they established?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR STANIC
utterances.text: I always invoke laws, Mr. President. This is regulated by law. If the state is attacked, either from the outside or the inside, certain bodies are established that will ensure the safety and security of citizens and make sure that they receive proper supplies and then the business community, companies, enterprises, so on, and I believe that all of this is regulated in legal provisions and I remember full well that Mr. Luketa and a few other lawyers analysed that then.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: What was the function of Mr. Luketa whom you mentioned?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR STANIC
utterances.text: Luketa was even before the war broke out the secretary -- the secretary -- he was actually a misdemeanors judge and then later on he became president of the court of the Municipal Assembly of Vogosca. So he was in charge of legal acts in Vogosca and as such had been co-opted into the Crisis Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. On page 44 of today's transcript, Mr. Tieger, in his compound questions, suggested that the Serb side or, rather, the SDS was preparing to firmly hold on to power throughout the municipality where Serbs are a majority and in municipalities where they are minority, that they would establish their own administration or some kind of government of their own. Did you know -- or, rather, were Muslims and Croats denied the right to establish their own municipalities where they had condition for that -- conditions for that?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR STANIC
utterances.text: No. On the contrary. When I was involved in negotiations on behalf of the Crisis Staff, I was authorised by the Crisis Staff from the Municipal Assembly of Vogosca and I offered them that we draw the border in a peaceful manner, that we respect each other until a definitive solution was reached. And why did I do this? Because of at time a conference had already started, an international conference, the purpose of which was to define the problems in Bosnia-Herzegovina in accordance with Cutileiro's plan, and before it was known as Lord Carrington's plan, and that was sometime in March 1992. It is then that this initiative was launched, and to be quite frank at the time I believed that war would not break out because all three factions, and you were also present in negotiations, all three factions agreed that a solution should be found in order to divide up the territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina and to form entities, if I'm not mistaken; if I am, do correct me.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did the Muslims in Vogosca have their own municipality in Vogosca?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR STANIC
utterances.text: The Muslims in Vogosca had their own municipality at Kobilja Glava and in that municipality -- that municipality included all inhabitants who were in Ugarsko, Ugljesici, Hotonj, Barice, Kobilja Glava. It included all those people who had left the core part of the city, the core part of the town of Vogosca, the urban part.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. As a municipality, was it your ambition for the Serbian municipality of Vogosca to include parts of the Muslim municipality of Vogosca, settlements that had a Muslim majority?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR STANIC
utterances.text: No, we didn't have such an intention at the outset. We didn't receive such ideas from anyone, and within the Crisis Staff this was not matter that we ever discussed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did the Muslim side have the ambition to place the Serbian neighbourhoods under its own control?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR STANIC
utterances.text: From the very beginning from April onwards, when they started taking civilians in the Grahovici village -- well, these people were civilians who weren't armed. From that point in time they used deception to take them in, to bring them in and even today we don't know what happened to them. That included Spasojevici, Pajdaci, Zivkovici, Vladusici, and so on and so forth. But that is the case, Mr. President. It can be seen by the following: Mile Palija, that is the first and last name of one of the persons in that group, he had a summer house in Grahovici, he was also arrested, but since he was a labourer and a good worker in Pretis, the Pretis company, a friend of his recognised him and he said, Mile you should flee from here, flee downstream otherwise you will all come to harm. What did that mean? Well, there was then the attack on Pretis on the 17th or 18th or the 20th I don't know exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: We'll get there later. THE INTERPRETERS: The speakers are kindly asked to slow down for the interpretation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I would like to ask you whether Mr. Trifunovic --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Please put a pause, both of you, for the benefit of the interpreters and us. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And I may make this marker now. I think we're already straying into area that stretch the boundaries of the cross-examination, and I will be rising to make that objection if it continues.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You'll see your Excellencies that that is not the case. On page 55 you were asked the following -- well, in fact, you were told that Mr. Trifunovic had asked that Kobilja Glava be liberated. Did Mr. Trifunovic -- was Mr. Trifunovic part of the civilian authorities? What was he a part of?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR STANIC
utterances.text: Mr. Trifunovic was a commander. He was the commander of the Blagovac Battalion. I don't know when this was presented, Mr. President. When I was there Mr. Trifunovic had certain tasks he had to carry out on behalf of the Crisis Staff. I told the Prosecution about that. He had to take care of Pretis. That was the military task that had been assigned to him when the mobilisation was carried out and he was to have good neighbourly relationships with the Tihovici local commune.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did Mr. Trifunovic have any military reasons to liberate Kobilja Glava?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR STANIC
utterances.text: No, by no means. He had no such reasons. And I am quite surprised that he gave such a statement to be quite frank.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And were you attacked from the area of Kobilja Glava?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR STANIC
utterances.text: There were incessant attacks from Kobilja Glava. The first one was the one launched on Pretis. That was on the 18th or 19th of April, and then there were attacks from Betanija, and there were incessant attacks on the municipality as well on the Crisis Staff headquarters in Kosinj and on the Hotel Park, and so on and so forth. So this was shelling from Kobilja Glava, Betanija, Ugorsko, I believe, and Ugljesici. So for those reasons as I have just said, we frequently change our location. We would move elsewhere in order to avoid being hit by shells and there were also attacks when a route was made from Pretis to Poljine and our convoys were incessantly attacked, our convoys that were transporting food and medicine for the population. Then there were vans that were transporting the civilians and the wounded which was also attacked, and so on and so forth, but I can't remember all the details because this happened a long time ago but that's what the situation was.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. What I have mentioned is something that Mr. Tieger showed you. On page 57 he showed you a document from the session of the Assembly. It was dated the 14th of November. Could we now have a look at 65 ter 15746. Could we see the first page in the English version. Do we agree that this was drafted on the 14th of November, 1992? It's regular combat report to the Main Staff of the Army of Republika Srpska. You see the date at the top, sir?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR STANIC
utterances.text: Yes, see the date but I can't see the text. I don't see what it is about.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I will read it out to save time. Paragraph 1 says: "The enemy periodically violated the agreed truce during the day with the most active attacks being towards Zuc and Orlic from the direction of Boljakov Potok and Kobilja Glava towards Vogosca. A sabotage group the strength of a squad also penetrated that axis." How does this fit in with the information you have about the activities in Kobilja Glava?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR STANIC
utterances.text: There was such action all the time from Kobilja Glava and beyond, and attacks were launched from Sarajevo against Zuc. And on the 10th of July, 1992, the Muslim forces took Zuc. They took the most elevated position on Zuc which is Orlic, and they drove back our forces. Zuc is inhabited exclusively by Serbs, and on that occasion they set fire to Zuc and our territorial forces went further down 50 to 60 metres further down and that is where they held that line.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. With regard to these attacks from Kobilja Glava, would that be the military reason for liberating Kobilja Glava regardless of the fact that you didn't want to include it?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Okay. Multiple things wrong with it. Number one, first, it was asked and answered, and then when the accused got an answer he didn't want, now he asks a leading question to the contrary. So I object to this approach once again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The Chamber absolutely agrees with your observation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Very well, I'll rephrase the question. I'll ask the following: Mr. Stanic, do you stand by what you said a little earlier that Mr. Trifunovic did not have any military reasons to go to Kobilja Glava?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR STANIC
utterances.text: I stand by that because he didn't even have the forces and in my opinion there would have been huge casualties amongst our people if he had. That's my position. Perhaps I'm mistaken, but there were reasons because from Betanija and Kobilja Glava there was incessant shelling of the Pretis neighbourhood and certainly between 30 and 40 people while I was in Vogosca died in Pretis because of these attacks from Kobilja Glava, but there were these reasons that it wasn't because of Miladin Trifunovic. It's just that there was an Operative Group that could have done this because we didn't have sufficient men for such purposes at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. At the level of the Vogosca Brigade or the corps was a military attempt made to liberate Kobilja Glava at any point in time?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR STANIC
utterances.text: No, this was never done.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Could this document please be admitted into evidence?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: No objection, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. Next Defence exhibit.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 15746 receives number D2680, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Stanic, when did you resign from your position as president of the municipality?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR STANIC
utterances.text: I resigned from my position as president of the municipality on the 14th of November, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could you we briefly have a look at P5511. Could we see the Serbian version, 1D20513; and the English version is P5511. The handwritten version in the Serbian language is the other document I referred to. Could we see the -- could we see 1D20513, the typewritten version, in fact, in Serbian and we can keep the translation on the screen. Thank you. The date is the 11th of November. Could we now see -- the 14th of November. I apologise. Could we now see page 6 in the Serbian version and it's probably the same page in the English version.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Stanic, could you please read out the part where it says "Stanisic." It's the first line from the bottom just before "Trifunovic." Stanisic requests and says.

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR STANIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, I can see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Could you read it out?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. Please wait till we have the -- please wait till we have the English page.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, that's it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Could you read it out loud. First Stanisic and then Trifunovic and then the second Stanisic.

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR STANIC
utterances.text: Stanisic: He is addressing all the present and informing them that he is giving an irrevocable resignation. He cannot sit in the municipal building and do nothing and be at the service of the army, so it is no wonder there is nothing in this municipality. And then I suffered enough. I do not want to be the president and you cannot retain me. Mr. President, those aren't my actual words. My actual words were quite different. If I may, and I remember this to this day, I resigned for the simple reason that I wouldn't allow certain criminal activities to take place. I wouldn't allow combatants at the lines to be at the lines for seven, eight dates and I wouldn't allow other people to enter their flats and houses. So I wanted to submit my resignation because there was a previous agreement according to which the president of the Executive Committee should be informed of his incorrect relationship to the Assembly. So they asked me to do this. As the president of the municipality I subjected myself to checks and then I told Mr. Rajko and President Krajisnik, President Momcilo Krajisnik, I said this is what is on the agenda. I read it out. Do you agree with it? We do. When I read it out -- after I had read it out and when these items were to be implemented we started firing on the President of the Executive Board -- well, then there was a dispute.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Very well. Could we just stop here briefly. You say that these minutes, the interpretation of the person who took the minutes but does it reflect what you in fact said, the substance of what you said; namely that you wouldn't remain and that they couldn't retain you there?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR STANIC
utterances.text: I said I'm tendering my irrevocable resignation and then the president of the National Assembly, Mr. Krajisnik, intervened and said that I should postpone my resignation for a month until the Executive Board adopted a working programme and a report on its work. He was supposed to do this in a timely manner.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR STANIC
utterances.text: I apologise, Mr. President. And then when Mr. Krajisnik intervened as well as the representatives who asked for me to stay on, I said, Very well, I'll postpone my resignation for a month until a new Assembly is held and until a new report on work is drafted. This has nothing to do with what I now see before me. This is the first time I have seen it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In paragraph 14 you were asked about the volunteers, and you yourself mentioned the association that was concerned. With regard to payment for volunteers in the unit, was this in any way different from the way in which conscripts who were called up were paid?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR STANIC
utterances.text: No. They had the same rights, the same salaries, the same benefits and when they were wounded, the rights of their families were enforced. The rights of a killed soldier had the right to disability. The families of those who had been killed had the rights to an allowance.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did the municipality pay a paramilitary group of any kind?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR STANIC
utterances.text: No. Never as far as I know. Never did it pay any paramilitary groups.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Under the law, what are the competencies, if any, are there on the municipality local commune, in terms of defence or a company?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR STANIC
utterances.text: What do you mean a company.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, did large companies have a role to play?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR STANIC
utterances.text: Yes, for example, like the Pretis factory. My organisation unit, the department of security within the company had between 60 and 80 members who were armed. Our manager was Risto Bajalo. The people had their weapons. Of course there was no artillery but infantry weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: What about local communes and municipalities, did they have any competencies in the domain of defence?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR STANIC
utterances.text: Yes. All local communes which were members of municipalities had a role to play in terms of securing their territory as part of the overall system of Territorial Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: When a new municipality was established, what were its obligations vis-a-vis Territorial Defence?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR STANIC
utterances.text: New municipalities acted in accordance with the law which was in place before the new municipality was formed. If there were changes and amendments to the law, then the municipalities and local communes had to harmonise their statutes with those. So the harmonisation of legal regulations and tasks had to be carried out in a precise way.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Please bear with me. You mentioned Pretis and its defence role. Could we have 1D6265. During cross-examination it was mentioned on page 53, line 11, the attack on Pretis. 1D6265. That's it. I will read out. Is it the 18th of April the document?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR STANIC
utterances.text: Well, the attack on Pretis was on the 17th or the 18th, whereas here I see the 18th. I always had a difficulty with -- with those two dates.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you know the person who signed this document, Mevludin Alic, from the Secretariat of National Defence?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR STANIC
utterances.text: I did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Were there still joint bodies in place at the time?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR STANIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. This is a document of Bosnia-Herzegovina signed by a Muslim person; correct?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR STANIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Very well. I'll read at -- well the top of the page is everything clear?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR STANIC
utterances.text: Yes, but I can't see the text itself well.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: But what are the bodies mentioned in the heading?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR STANIC
utterances.text: The town information centre in Sarajevo. Subject, report, the date is the 18th of April. The number is 02/33, and then something I can't read.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Very well. So it was sent to the city information centre but who sent it?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR STANIC
utterances.text: Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, Vogosca municipality, municipal Secretariat for National Defence, information centre.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Was it still the joint municipality of Vogosca or the Muslim municipality of Vogosca?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter did not hear the witness's answer. There should be a pause.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, your conversation just simply moves too fast for the interpreters to keep up. Please put a pause again. The answer of the witness was not heard by the interpreters. Could we repeat from there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: When I asked you if it was still the joint municipality or the Muslim municipality of Vogosca your answer was not heard.

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR STANIC
utterances.text: It was the joint municipality. The authorities comprised both Muslims and Serbs at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Reading from the first paragraph at about 400 hours in the morning on the 18th of April, 1992, a convoy of approximately ten trucks came from the direction of Sarajevo and went through the front entrance of Pretis disarming two security officers in the process. The trucks went on to the warehouse of the Kones basic organisation of associated labour where ammunition was loaded on the trucks and which was then taken towards the exit. On the way to the exit they were attacked by Pretis security officers and fighting ensued. Inhabitants of Blagovac local commune and Hotonj local commune subsequently joined the fighting. All this happened between 600 and 630 hours. Does the document reflect what you had to say about the attack?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR STANIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Whose trucks could have arrived from the direction of Sarajevo on the 18th of April?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR STANIC
utterances.text: What I kept repeating was that only the Patriotic League could come from that direction. It was a military formation of the SDA party. They had their insignia and structure. They were the ones who went through the gate.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. We can see that some inhabitants of Blagovac took part. Who was in the majority there?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR STANIC
utterances.text: Blagovac has 98 per cent of Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So we see the inhabitants of Hotonj taking part too. Who was in the majority there?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR STANIC
utterances.text: Hotonj, well, some took part. The majority population in Hotonj is Muslim.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I seek to tender this?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document -- document 1D6265 receives number D2681, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did you have a Serb paramilitary or any other kind of military organisation in Vogosca at the time?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR STANIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: What were your expectations of the JNA in that regard? Please pause. What were your expectations on the part of the JNA?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR STANIC
utterances.text: Well, I expected they would take prompt reaction, but only later once Pretis had been defended they arrived taking over the gate and the factory itself with a lieutenant-colonel. It was around 1.30 or 2.00 when everything had already stopped, all the fighting. It would have been critical if the fighting had continued, because we did not have enough strength to defend Pretis. Otherwise, it would have been taken by the Patriotic League, the paramilitaries.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Overall, what were the expectations of Serbs in Vogosca given the fact that they did not have their own paramilitary unit? What did they expect the JNA to do in case of attack?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR STANIC
utterances.text: In case of an attack, it had to strike speedily and timely, because it was a JNA facility and they were supposed to guard it, which is what they had done up until a certain time. They had to react more quickly, but they didn't. They only arrived before 2.00. We called you and the late Koljevic and Krajisnik to take part so that the command would provide reinforcements to secure Pretis as it was vital to the population and Republika Srpska as well as Bosnia-Herzegovina. We didn't know things would develop that way. We feared that it would fall in the wrong hands because there was a lot of explosives there, and in case it was taken over by the Patriotic League, it could have blown the whole thing up. It would have been a disaster.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You said you contacted me. Could we have P5720. It was the same date, and we can see my reaction in it. P5720.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I'm going to wait to look at the document, but this may have been a time to rise and wonder exactly how this aspect of redirect arises from cross.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Can I hear from you, Mr. Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] On page 53, I believe, there was a question about the attack on Pretis. My learned friend Mr. Tieger found it necessary to check during his cross-examination some things from the statement. The question had to do about the position of the first Serb leadership concerning the industrial facilities in Vogosca.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. Let us hear the question.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can we have the next page. The 18th of April is the date. Please take note.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: The third or fourth line from the top, Radovan Karadzic is talking to Milutin Kukanjac. Who was he?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR STANIC
utterances.text: General Milutin Kukanjac was the commander of the Sarajevo Army District, as far as I recall and if I'm not mistaken.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. So Karadzic: As for Vogosca, please, do see what was going on there. Vikic and the Green Berets there are trying to take Pretis to get ahold of the assets. Kukanjac said: That has to be stopped. In the English it is at the bottom of the page. So he said: It must be stopped. Could we go to the next page in the English. In the Serbian Karadzic says: Our people there are defending it. We're working on it. Kukanjac said: Let them defend it. Can we have the next page in the Serbian version.
